findings.title: Silent arbitrary crypto provider selection when multiple providers have equal order
findings.body: detectProvider now sorts providers by order and always returns the first one instead of throwing when multiple providers are present. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so if more than one of them is on the classpath the chosen provider depends on unspecified ServiceLoader enumeration order. Previously this condition failed fast. With this change a non-FIPS provider can be selected on a FIPS-enabled classpath, or the FIPS provider constructor can still run and modify security providers before it is ignored. This can violate FIPS requirements and is very hard to diagnose because other providers are only logged at debug level.

findings.title: Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public interface. Adding an abstract int order() method without a default implementation breaks both source and binary compatibility for any third-party or otherwise out-of-tree implementation of CryptoProvider; such implementations will fail to compile or will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime. The method should have a default implementation, for example returning a neutral order, unless this is a deliberately accepted breaking API change.

findings.title: Registered crypto provider throws UnsupportedOperationException for core crypto operations
findings.body: AuthzClientCryptoProvider is advertised through META-INF/services and will be auto-selected when no higher-order provider is present. Yet getSignature(), getKeyPairGen(), getKeyFactory(), getCertificateUtils(), getPemUtils(), and most other CryptoProvider methods throw UnsupportedOperationException. Standalone authz-client code that uses these SPI methods, such as JWT client authentication or other signature operations via CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getSignature(...), will fail at runtime instead of using the JCA defaults. Either implement the needed methods using standard JCA or do not register a class as a general CryptoProvider until it is complete.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() documents that it returns a BouncyCastle security provider. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is typically the JDK SUN/SunJSSE provider when BC is not present. Any caller that relies on the returned provider being BC, for BC algorithms or provider-specific registration, gets the wrong provider, which can lead to algorithm lookup failures or inconsistent provider behavior. The provider should return the actual BC provider it uses, or null if it intentionally does not use BC, with callers updated accordingly.

findings.title: ECDSA conversion test uses one default EC key for all curves and only tests round-trip
findings.body: The test generates a single KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() without specifying a curve. For ES384 and ES512 the key is not necessarily on P-384 or P-521, and the test only asserts that DER -> R||S -> DER equals the intermediate R||S. It does not verify the conversions against the JCA signature value or against known test vectors, so an incorrect implementation could pass while producing wrong encodings for the actual algorithm or curve. Use per-algorithm curve parameters and assert the expected raw signature/conversion result.
